extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and agents practicing before the USPTO (patent and trademark practitioners); counsel subject to USPTO OED discipline procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements governing attorney/agent conduct before the USPTO, including signature/specimen authenticity for trademark filings, limits on limited-recognition patent practice, supervision of non-practitioner assistants, candor to OED/tribunal, and sanctions/reinstatement procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal-signature requirement for trademark filings (TEAS / 18 U.S.C. §1001)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark applications and related documents (e.g., responses to Office Actions, CAR forms) contain declarations that must be personally signed by the named signatory and are submitted under penalty of perjury pursuant to 18 U.S.C. §1001. The USPTO relies on these material factual assertions in deciding registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must not substitute typed signatures for hand-signed signatures and must ensure any hand-signed declarations uploaded to TEAS were actually signed by the named signatories. Examples of noncompliance include filing declarations that were not personally signed by the named signatory. Submission of such inauthentic signatures can expose the filer to discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable inquiry under 37 C.F.R. §11.18 to verify authenticity of signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: By submitting signed declarations and other signature-bearing documents to the USPTO, a practitioner certifies that, to the best of the practitioner's knowledge after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances, the signatures were personally signed by the named signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable inquiry requires the practitioner to implement adequate controls and measures when receiving signatures (especially from third parties or foreign-based entities). Examples of reasonable-care failures: accepting batches of purported signatures without checking uniqueness, failing to compare obvious duplicates, and otherwise relying unquestioningly on referring entities to procure signatures. Obvious red flags (identical signatures across different applicants, implausible signer information) must trigger further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specimen authenticity and actual use requirement for 15 U.S.C. §1051(a) applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark applications filed on a 15 U.S.C. §1051(a) (use in commerce) basis must include a specimen showing the applied-for mark as actually used in commerce for each class listed in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners submitting specimens must, consistent with 37 C.F.R. §11.18, conduct a reasonable inquiry into the authenticity of specimens and whether they demonstrate actual use in commerce. Examples of suspicious specimens include multiple filings with screenshots from the same website with repeated or implausible customer invoice information (e.g., same single-name customer, inconsistent zip codes). Failure to investigate such indicia of falsity constitutes misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision of non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. §11.503(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must make reasonable efforts to ensure that the conduct of non-practitioner assistants is compatible with the practitioner's professional obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing or relying on non-practitioner assistants (including foreign-based entities or non-practitioner employees of referring agents), practitioners must implement measures and controls to verify the authenticity of signatures, declarations, and specimens those assistants provide. Failing to put such supervisory controls in place (e.g., simply accepting third-party-prepared documents without verification) violates §11.503(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence obligation (37 C.F.R. §11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must provide competent representation to clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent representation includes conducting necessary inquiries into the authenticity of signatures and specimens, implementing adequate controls when working with third parties, and ensuring filings satisfy statutory/regulatory requirements. The Final Order treats failures to verify signatures and specimens and failures to implement controls as violations of §11.101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence obligation (37 C.F.R. §11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must act with reasonable diligence in representing clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence includes timely and adequate review of filings and supporting materials (signatures, specimens) before submission. Routinely filing documents without sufficient review (including mass-filing suspicious documents with identical indicia) is a violation of §11.103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor to the tribunal / ex parte disclosure obligations (37 C.F.R. §11.303)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an ex parte proceeding, a practitioner must not knowingly fail to inform the tribunal of all material facts known to the practitioner that would enable the tribunal to make an informed decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting inauthentic declarations and false specimens in trademark proceedings (thereby withholding material facts about authenticity) violates the candor rule. Practitioners must not certify authenticity without conducting reasonable inquiry; knowingly certifying false material facts violates §11.303(a) and (d).

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements and failures to correct misapprehensions in registration/disciplinary matters (37 C.F.R. §§11.801(a),(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is prohibited to knowingly make a false statement of material fact in connection with an application for registration or recognition or a disciplinary matter, and to fail to disclose facts necessary to correct a misapprehension known to have arisen in such an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During applications for limited recognition or in OED investigations, practitioners must provide truthful, complete information and promptly correct known misapprehensions. Examples of misconduct: falsely representing the existence of an affiliated registered practitioner, falsely stating employment relationships, submitting altered documents to mislead OED.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized practice before the USPTO and compliance with limited-recognition terms (37 C.F.R. §§11.9(b) and 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonimmigrant aliens granted limited recognition under 37 C.F.R. §11.9(b) may be authorized only to prepare and prosecute patent applications for and represent patent applicants who are clients of the authorized employer, and such grants may include conditions (e.g., a registered practitioner affiliated with the employer must be of record). Practicing outside those terms constitutes unauthorized practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited-recognition practitioners must ensure that: (1) their patent practice is for the employer's clients as authorized; (2) a registered practitioner affiliated with the employer serves as an attorney of record on each patent matter when required; and (3) public representations reflect limited recognition status. Acting as sole attorney of record for matters that are not clients of the authorized employer, or holding oneself out as a full registered practitioner contrary to grant conditions, violates §11.505 and the terms of the grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications and advertising rules (37 C.F.R. §11.701) — disclosure of limited recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications about the practitioner's services must be truthful and not misleading. When practicing under limited recognition, any published biographical or advertising information regarding the practitioner's ability to practice in patent matters must indicate the limited recognition status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners with limited recognition must include clear disclosure of their limited status in web listings, advertisements, and other public materials. Failing to disclose limited recognition while advertising patent services or holding oneself out as a registered patent attorney violates §11.701.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. §11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples include submitting inauthentic declarations and false specimens, providing altered documents to mislead OED, and making knowingly false statements during application or investigation processes. Such conduct is a standalone basis for discipline under §11.804(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. §11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting false evidence, engaging in unauthorized practice, making false statements to OED, or otherwise undermining institutional processes supports a finding under §11.804(d). The rule is applied where misconduct significantly impairs fair administration of USPTO processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to OED investigations—use of RFIs and requirements under 37 C.F.R. §11.22(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: OED may issue a Response for Information and Evidence (RFI) under 37 C.F.R. §11.22(f) requesting details about a practitioner's compliance with grants or conduct; practitioners must respond truthfully and fully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: False or misleading responses to RFIs (e.g., misrepresenting employer relationships or the role of affiliated practitioners) constitute separate violations. Practitioners should preserve documents, provide accurate exhibits, and not alter materials to mislead investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions, suspension, probation enforcement procedures, and Order to Show Cause (related to 37 C.F.R. §§11.58, 11.60 and OED enforcement practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO may suspend a practitioner, require compliance with notice and client-protection provisions (37 C.F.R. §11.58), impose probation with monitoring requirements, and issue Orders to Show Cause for alleged probationary violations; reinstatement requires a petition under 37 C.F.R. §11.60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions can include suspension for a specified period, conditions on reapplication for registration, probation with reporting (e.g., bi-weekly trademark searches and bi-monthly reports), and additional suspension if probation terms are violated. The OED Director may issue an Order to Show Cause, provide time to respond, and seek additional suspension based on the response and supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client-notice and client-transfer obligations during suspension (37 C.F.R. §11.58 and related conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended practitioner must comply with 37 C.F.R. §11.58, including notifying clients of suspension and taking steps to protect client interests (e.g., providing notice and copies of orders). The Final Order specifies procedures for foreign-domiciled clients (translated notices, acceptable transmission methods, and required affidavits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable methods for notifying foreign-domiciled clients include emailing the client's email address (if reasonably believed to be directly accessible by the client), emailing an address belonging to the client, or emailing the foreign referring entity only if the practitioner takes reasonable measures to ensure the entity forwards the translated Final Order to the client and confirms receipt. The practitioner's affidavit must detail the measures taken; failure to comply can be enforced during probation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions and prohibitions on USPTO electronic system access while suspended
rubrics_metrics.description: While suspended (and until reinstated), a practitioner may be prohibited from applying for, activating, using, or sponsoring USPTO.gov electronic system accounts or from verifying others' credentials for such accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practitioner must not obtain a USPTO verified Electronic System account, have his name added to such an account, verify others' credentials, or sponsor account access until reinstated. The USPTO is authorized to disallow such access and the practitioner bears responsibility for any re-activation efforts after reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement conditions and continuing legal education requirement (37 C.F.R. §11.60; 28 U.S.C. §1746 affidavit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reinstatement to practice requires filing a petition under 37 C.F.R. §11.60 and, as a condition, submission of a declaration/affidavit (in compliance with 28 U.S.C. §1746) that the practitioner has completed specified CLE credits: five hours on ethics/professional responsibility and five hours on intellectual property law (as set in this Final Order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practitioner must submit the certified affidavit/declaration as part of any reinstatement petition and comply with any additional conditions set by OED. The Final Order ties reinstatement eligibility to compliance with these education requirements and other terms of the order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and public notice of disciplinary action
rubrics_metrics.description: Final Orders and material notices of suspension/probation are published by OED (electronic FOIA Reading Room) and may be published in the Official Gazette with a notice materially consistent with the Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should expect public disclosure of disciplinary actions and that such publications may be used as an aggravating factor in future proceedings. The practitioner’s agreement to settlement may also include waivers of rights to seek reconsideration or appeal, which the Office will memorialize in the published notice.
